result:
`final.py` is a LIRS cache, and it scores 0.5647 on the search split, against the 0.365 baseline. I used 6 of the 24 scorer calls and about 5 minutes of the roughly 15-minute budget. I stopped early because the last four variants all landed between 0.560 and 0.564. I did not score on a held-out split. The "held" numbers in my own harness were not independent of tuning, so the score on unseen instances may differ.

LIRS keeps the keys that have been re-referenced recently, and it tracks recently evicted keys in a ghost list so a returning key is promoted quickly. That makes it resistant to one-off scans and to loops larger than the cache, which LRU handles worst. `final.py` reserves 5% of capacity for new, unproven keys and bounds the tracking stack at 3 × capacity.

| Candidate | Search score |
|---|---|
| LRU baseline | 0.365 |
| LIRS, 5% reserve, stack 3 × capacity (`final.py`) | **0.5647** |
| LIRS, 2% reserve, stack 8 × capacity | 0.5634 |
| LIRS, 1% reserve, stack 6 × capacity | 0.5638 |
| LIRS plus a frequency-based admission filter | 0.5594 |
| LIRS plus frequency-aware choice of which new key to evict | 0.5604 |
| Window cache with frequency-based admission (TinyLFU-style) | 0.5034 |

- **Where it is weak:** the `hot_with_scans` and `mixed` traces stay at about 0.24–0.26 for every LIRS variant. The TinyLFU-style cache did slightly better there (0.247 and 0.270) but much worse on `recency` (0.60 vs 0.80), so it lost overall.
- **Tuning:** the reserve size and stack bound made almost no difference, so I kept the first setting.
- **Local harness:** I generated mixed traces with hot keys, loops, scans and popularity shifts. It ranked the candidates in the same order as the scorer except for the TinyLFU-style cache, which it ranked well below LIRS (0.33 vs 0.42) while the scorer ranked it just a little lower (0.503 vs 0.565).

I did not run the 15 timing-limited checks on the full set of unseen traces. On my own 5 traces the final file ran in about 1 second.
